objective: By the end of this lesson you can spot the signs of common aeromedical problems, say what causes them and what to do, know the alcohol and drug rules, and decide honestly if you are fit to fly.
why: About 80 percent of aviation accidents are tied to human factors, not the airplane [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]. Checking yourself is as important as checking the airplane [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1h]].

prereading.what: Hypoxia, hyperventilation, ears and sinuses, disorientation, illusions, motion sickness, CO, stress, fatigue, dehydration, alcohol, drugs, scuba diving.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 17, 17-3 to 17-19

prereading.what: Hazardous attitudes and antidotes, IMSAFE, PAVE, personal minimums.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 2, 2-5 to 2-10

prereading.what: Fitness for flight, effects of altitude, scuba waits, CO, illusions.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-1 to 8-1-5

warmup: You slept 5 hours, have a stuffy nose, and your friends are waiting at the airport for a sunset flight. What is the first thing you should check before you even look at the weather?

key_terms.def: Not enough oxygen for the body, most dangerous for the brain [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].
Breathing too fast and deep, so the body loses too much carbon dioxide [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Not knowing the airplane's attitude, position or movement because your senses disagree [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
Time you have to make and carry out life-saving decisions at an altitude without extra oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Personal checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].
One of five thinking patterns that lead to bad decisions: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, resignation [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].
Single-Pilot Resource Management: using every resource, inside and outside the aircraft, to make the flight end well [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].
Crew Resource Management: using all people, equipment and information to work as a crew and decide well [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]].
Accurately knowing everything about the pilot, aircraft, environment and operation that affects safety [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Seeing or hearing what you expect, and keeping a wrong picture even when the evidence says otherwise [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].
Pushing away information that does not fit what you already believe [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].
Your own limits, stricter than the regulations, based on your experience and skill [[30:13|RMH 2-1]].

body.p: Hypoxia means "not enough oxygen." The brain is hurt first, so even mild hypoxia can cause deadly mistakes [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. The air is still about 21 percent oxygen at altitude; there is just less pressure pushing it into your lungs [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]].

Symptoms vary by person: blue fingernails and lips (cyanosis), headache, slow reactions, impaired judgment, euphoria, vision problems, drowsiness, dizziness, tingling, numbness. Worst of all, you may feel fine [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

bullets: Night vision gets worse at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]].
From 12,000 to 15,000 feet, judgment, memory, alertness and coordination are impaired [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]].
Performance can seriously drop within 15 minutes at 15,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]].
Smoking, CO, anemia, alcohol and some medicines make hypoxia start lower [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]].

body.p: Values from [[1:426|PHAK Figure 17-1]]. Fix: descend and/or use supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.211: above 12,500 ft MSL up to and including 14,000 ft MSL cabin pressure altitude, the required minimum flight crew must have and use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that lasts more than 30 minutes; above 14,000 ft, the whole time; above 15,000 ft, each occupant must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. AIM advice: use oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a]].

check.q: Which type of hypoxia does carbon monoxide cause?
check.a: Hypemic hypoxia. CO keeps the blood from carrying oxygen [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].

body.p: Hyperventilation is breathing too fast and too deep, so you blow off too much carbon dioxide. Stress or a surprise can trigger it without you noticing [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

bullets: Symptoms: vision problems, lightheaded or dizzy, tingling, hot and cold feelings, muscle spasms, even unconsciousness [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].
Fix: slow your breathing on purpose. Talking out loud or breathing into a paper bag helps. Recovery is usually fast [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Hypoxia and hyperventilation feel alike and can happen together. If you are on oxygen, set it to 100 percent, check the system works, then slow your breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

check.q: You feel tingling and dizzy right after a near-miss at 3,000 feet with no oxygen system. Most likely cause and fix?
check.a: Hyperventilation from stress. Consciously slow your breathing rate and depth, or talk out loud [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

body.p: Gas trapped in body spaces expands and shrinks as you climb and descend. The Eustachian tube links each middle ear to your throat and lets pressure equalize [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

bullets: Climbing: air escapes on its own. Descending: you must open the tube by swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva maneuver (close mouth, pinch nose, blow gently) [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]].
A cold, sore throat or allergies can block the tube. Ear block can cause severe pain, hearing loss, even a ruptured eardrum [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]].
Sinus block happens most often during descent, with sharp pain above the eyebrows or in the cheeks (upper teeth may ache). Slow descent rates reduce the pain [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Best prevention: don't fly with a cold or nasal allergy. Sprays and drops usually don't protect enough, and oral decongestants can impair you. If it doesn't clear soon after landing, see a doctor [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]].

check.q: Is ear block more likely in the climb or the descent?
check.a: Descent. Air escapes on its own when climbing, but in descent you must open the Eustachian tube yourself [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]].

body.p: Your brain uses three systems for balance: the inner ear (vestibular), nerves in skin, muscles and joints ("seat of the pants"), and your eyes. Without outside visual cues, as in clouds, the other two can fool you fast [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

The inner ear's canals can't sense a rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower, so a slow, gradual turn entry goes unnoticed [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Once a turn is steady, the fluid moves at the same speed as the canal wall and you feel no turn at all [[1:429|PHAK Figure 17-4]].

head: Illusion
What you feel
Danger
rows: Banked the other way after leveling from a slow turn
Leaning toward, or rolling back into, the original turn [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]]
Tumbling on another axis after a head move in a long turn
Wings level while descending in a steady turn
Tumbling backward after climb to level

callout.text: Trust the instruments, not your body. Avoid sudden head movement, avoid flight without a visible horizon unless trained [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]], and remember illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue and mild hypoxia raise your risk [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

check.q: In a long, steady turn in clouds you drop a pen and bend down to grab it. What illusion is likely?
check.a: Coriolis illusion. Keep head movement small and retrieve objects carefully [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

body.p: Visual illusions mostly hit you on landing. Each one makes you think you're higher or lower than you are [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

Night illusions: a false horizon from sloping clouds or ground lights [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]; autokinesis, where a stared-at light seems to move after about 8 to 10 seconds, so don't stare at a light more than 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]].

callout.text: Prevent landing errors: expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, check the Chart Supplement for slope and lighting, check the altimeter often, and use VASI/PAPI when available [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

check.q: You're landing on a runway much narrower than you're used to. What will you tend to do?
check.a: Fly a lower approach, because you feel higher than you are [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

body.p: Motion sickness comes from the brain getting mixed messages. Symptoms: discomfort, nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating, vomiting. It usually goes away in the first few lessons and says nothing about your ability [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

bullets: Open fresh air vents, look at objects outside, avoid unneeded head movement [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
Tell your instructor; start with shorter flights in smooth air [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
Don't take motion-sickness pills like Dramamine to fly; they cause drowsiness [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

body.p: Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless and odorless. It sticks to blood about 200 times more easily than oxygen and causes hypemic hypoxia. The body needs up to 48 hours to clear it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Most light-aircraft heaters warm air over the exhaust manifold, so a cracked exhaust can leak CO into the cabin [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

bullets: Signs: exhaust smell, headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness, loss of muscle power [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
Action: heater off, fresh air vents and windows open, oxygen if available [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]; get medical care if symptoms are severe or last after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

callout.text: No smell does not mean no CO. A cheap CO detector changes color to warn you [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

check.q: Cruising in winter with the heat on, you get a headache and feel sleepy. What do you do?
check.a: Suspect CO: turn the heater off, open fresh air vents and windows, use oxygen if available, land and get checked [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

body.p: Stress is the body's response to demands. Acute stress is short-term (fight or flight). Chronic stress builds from ongoing problems like money, work or relationships, and performance falls sharply. A pilot with chronic stress should not fly and should see a doctor [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
Stress isn't on the regulations' grounding list, but it still hurts performance [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. When life is harder than usual, think about delaying the flight [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1f]].

bullets: In flight, AC 60-22 says: avoid distractions from flying the airplane, reduce your workload, and if an emergency happens, stay calm: think for a moment, weigh the alternatives, then act [[9:21|AC 60-22 par. 21e]].
Know and respect your personal limits. If flying itself adds to your stress, stop flying or get professional help [[9:21|AC 60-22 par. 21e]].

head: Acute fatigue
Chronic fatigue
rows: Strenuous effort, excitement, lack of sleep [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Not enough recovery between bouts of acute fatigue [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]
Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Long rest [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]]; usually needs a doctor [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]

bullets: Fatigue hurts attention, coordination and communication [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].
It may not be noticed until serious errors are made [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]].
If you are tired, stay on the ground. No training overcomes it in flight [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

check.q: What is the only way to prevent fatigue?

body.p: Dehydration is a critical loss of body water from hot cockpits, wind, humidity, and diuretic drinks like coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated soda. The first effect is fatigue; also headache, cramps, sleepiness, dizziness [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

bullets: Drink two to four quarts of water every 24 hours [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
You feel thirsty only after about a 1.5 quart deficit, so don't wait for thirst [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
On long hot flights: one quart per hour in severe heat, one pint per hour in moderate heat [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Heatstroke is the body losing control of its temperature; it can show up only as sudden collapse [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

body.p: Nutrition: eat regular balanced meals, bring snacks and water [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Missed meals lead to low blood sugar, a physical stressor [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. AC 60-22's preflight fitness checklist asks: Have I eaten a sensible meal with protein? Do I have a protein snack (cheese, meat or nuts) aboard? Am I dehydrated; do I need noncarbonated liquids like water or juice? Its version of I'M SAFE uses E for Eating: have I eaten enough of the proper foods to stay nourished for the whole flight? [[9:21|AC 60-22 par. 21f]] [[9:24|AC 60-22 Figure 7]]

Cold: cold reduces circulation to hands and feet (a form of stagnant hypoxia) [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and extreme heat or cold raises the body's oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a]]. Over remote areas, carry clothing, water and survival gear in case of a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

callout.text: The provided FAA handbooks, AIM and AC 60-22 do not describe hypothermia symptoms or treatment (AC 60-22 only asks if you have appropriate clothing [[9:21|AC 60-22 par. 21f]]). Your CFI will cover this from other sources.

check.q: Why shouldn't you rely on thirst to stay hydrated?
check.a: Thirst starts late (about a 1.5 quart deficit) and is turned off too easily by a small sip [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

body.p: Diving pushes extra nitrogen into your body. Flying too soon lowers the pressure and the nitrogen can form bubbles: decompression sickness, a serious in-flight emergency [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]]. Joint pain ("the bends") is the most common symptom [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Source: [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]] and [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. These are actual flight altitudes, not cabin altitudes, in case the cabin loses pressure.

callout.text: "12 low, 24 high or with stops." This applies to passengers too [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]].

check.q: Your passenger made a no-stop dive this morning. You plan to cruise at 9,500 ft. How long must they wait?
check.a: At least 24 hours, because the flight is above 8,000 ft [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.17(a): no one may act or attempt to act as a crewmember (1) within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol, (2) while under the influence of alcohol, (3) while using any drug that affects faculties contrary to safety, or (4) with alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

bullets: Both limits apply: 8 hours AND below 0.04. After 8 hours at 0.04 or higher you still can't fly [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Except in an emergency, don't carry a passenger who appears drunk or on drugs (medical patients under care excepted) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

You must take an alcohol test when a law officer asks under 91.17(c) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)]]. Refusing can mean denial of applications for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]] [[60:203|14 CFR 61.16(a)-(b)]].
Don't knowingly fly with illegal drugs aboard unless authorized [[60:438|14 CFR 91.19]].

If you hold a medical certificate, you can't act as PIC or required crew if you know or have reason to know of a medical condition, or take medication or treatment for one, that would make you fail your medical standards [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]].

head: 14 CFR 61.15 offense
Possible result
rows: Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension/revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15(a)]]
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension/revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(b)]]
Second DUI-type motor vehicle action within 3 years
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension/revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(d)]]
Not reporting a motor vehicle action
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension/revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(f)]]

callout.text: Report every alcohol/drug motor vehicle action (conviction, or license suspended, revoked, cancelled or denied) to the FAA Security office in writing within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

body.p: Marijuana: even where a state allows it, the FAA says its use by airmen is prohibited [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

check.q: You had one beer 9 hours ago and a breath test shows 0.02. Legal to fly?
check.a: Yes by 91.17, if you are not under the influence: more than 8 hours and under 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. But AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

chunks.title: Effects of alcohol, drugs and OTC medicine

body.p: As little as one ounce of liquor, one beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]]. Alcohol hurts judgment, coordination, vision, memory and attention [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

bullets: The body needs about 3 hours to clear one drink; large amounts can stay over 16 hours [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
AC 60-22 adds: several drinks affect thought and reaction for about 24 hours, and heavy drinking can linger 36 hours or longer [[9:23|AC 60-22 par. 25a]].
A hangover still means you're under the influence [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
At altitude, two drinks can act like three or four. Alcohol causes histotoxic hypoxia [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
One ounce of alcohol can equal an extra 2,000 feet of physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Alcohol can disturb the inner ear and cause disorientation for up to 48 hours [[1:439|PHAK Figure 17-9]].

body.p: Medicines: sedatives, tranquilizers, strong pain relievers and cough suppressants can impair judgment, memory, alertness and coordination. Antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and motion-sickness pills can too. Anything that depresses the nervous system makes hypoxia worse [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

bullets: Antihistamines and decongestants are common OTC drugs that can cause drowsiness. Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) stays in your system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
OTC aspirin, acetaminophen and ibuprofen usually don't restrict flying at correct doses; prescription painkillers almost always do [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
New medicine (OTC or prescribed): wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to check for side effects [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Sedating drugs: wait at least five dosing intervals (a 5-6 hour interval means 30 hours) [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Never mix drugs with alcohol, and don't take more than one drug unless a doctor prescribed it [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

callout.text: Safest rule: don't fly while taking any medication unless the FAA approves it. When in doubt, ask an AME [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. The condition you're treating may ground you too [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1c]].

check.q: You took a new allergy pill for the first time this morning. When can you fly?
check.a: Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to see if you have side effects; if it's sedating, also wait five dosing intervals after the last dose [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

body.p: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) is a systematic way to pick the best action for the situation [[1:40|PHAK 2-1]]. Good judgment can be taught; it isn't just a by-product of experience [[9:6|AC 60-22 par. 1]].

CRM is how a crew uses all people, equipment and information to decide well [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]] [[9:2|AC 60-22 par. 5d]]. SRM applies the same ideas when you fly alone: use ATC, the autopilot, checklists, even passengers [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

head: Tool
Steps
Use it for
rows: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]]
Check at key points in flight

body.p: Do a 5P check at least five times: preflight, before takeoff, mid-flight (hourly if over 2 hours), before descent, and before the final approach fix or entering the pattern [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]] [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]] [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

bullets: Inside resources: checklists, the POH, your passengers (traffic watch, reading checklists) [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].
Outside resources: ATC and Flight Service are the best [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].
External pressure is the risk that makes pilots ignore all the others. Plan for delays [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
One bad decision often leads to another (the poor judgment chain). ADM aims to break the chain early [[9:3|AC 60-22 par. 5h]].

callout.text: "If you find yourself saying it will 'probably' be okay, it is definitely time for a reality check" [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]].

check.q: In the TEAM checklist, what does it mean to "transfer" a risk?
check.a: Hand the decision or risk to someone better placed, such as a chief flight instructor or another pilot as PIC [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]].

body.p: Five attitudes lead to bad decisions [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Recognize the thought, label it hazardous, then say the antidote. Memorize them so they come automatically [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

head: Attitude
Sounds like
Antidote
rows: Follow the rules. They are usually right.
I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.

body.p: Table from [[1:44|PHAK Figure 2-4]]; AC 60-22 gives the same five attitudes and antidotes [[9:14|AC 60-22 par. 13]] [[9:15|AC 60-22 Figure 4]]. RMH names two attitudes that may come into play when a threat calls for a decision: impulsivity (acting without due thought) and resignation (not acting in time) [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

callout.text: Probably the two most dangerous words in aviation: "Watch this!" (Macho) [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

check.q: A pilot says, "The weather's going down, but nothing I do will change it, so I'll keep going." Which attitude and antidote?
check.a: Resignation. Antidote: "I'm not helpless. I can make a difference." [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]

body.p: Situational awareness is knowing what is going on and what's coming. Fatigue, stress and work overload make you fixate on one thing and lose the big picture. Many accidents start with a small distraction, like a gauge reading wrong, while the pilot stops flying the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

bullets: Plan, prioritize and sequence tasks. Do checklists, set radios and listen to ATIS early, during low workload [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
First sign of overload: working harder but getting less done [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
When overloaded: stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Feeling rushed? Ask ATC for a delay or vectors to buy time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

callout.text: Door pops open after takeoff? Fly the airplane. Don't rush to land or unbuckle to reach it. Open-door accidents come from distraction, not the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: What should a pilot do first when task saturation sets in?
check.a: Stop, think, slow down, and prioritize, keeping aircraft control first [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

body.p: Expectation bias: you keep a wrong picture even when evidence says otherwise. Example: an airline crew landed at the wrong airport at night because they expected it to be the right one and didn't check their displays [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

Confirmation bias: you push away information that doesn't fit what you already believe, instead of thinking "uh-oh." Both keep you on a plan the clues say is wrong. Fatigue makes both worse [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

bullets: Common while taxiing: you hear the clearance you usually get, not the one ATC gave [[30:46|RMH 6-3]] [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].
Read back and question any mismatch; ask for clarification [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Verify the runway and airport with your instruments, not just your eyes, especially at night [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

check.q: A NOTAM changed which parallel runway is closed, but you start an approach to the closed one anyway because it "used to be" open. Which bias?
check.a: Expectation bias. The pilot read the NOTAM but perceived it as it had been before [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

chunks.title: Managing aeromedical risk: IMSAFE and personal minimums

body.p: Pilot impairment causes more accidents than aircraft system failures, so preflight yourself like the airplane [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1h]].

head: IMSAFE
Ask yourself
rows: Am I taking anything that affects judgment or makes me drowsy? [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]
Pressure from work, money, health or family? [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]
Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours? [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]
Am I tired and not rested? [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]

body.p: Personal minimums are your own limits, stricter than the rules [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]. Set them on the ground, when no trip is pressing, then stick to them [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

bullets: For each special condition (illness, medication, stress, fatigue, not current, unfamiliar airplane or airport, outside pressure), raise your minimums: add at least 500 feet to ceiling, 1/2 mile to visibility, 500 feet to runway length, and subtract 5 knots from winds [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]].
Don't adjust minimums to make a specific flight happen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Talk to a CFI before any big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: Not sure about an illness? The safest rule is not to fly; ask an AME if that seems too strict [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1b]]. A quick test from AC 60-22: "Could I pass my medical examination right now?" If the answer isn't an absolute yes, don't fly [[9:21|AC 60-22 par. 21f]].

check.q: When is the right time to set or change personal minimums?
check.a: On the ground with time to think, never while under pressure to make a flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

chunks.title: Checkride skills: link symptoms to causes and fixes

body.p: The examiner will name symptoms (or a condition) and expect you to give the cause and corrective action for at least three conditions. Then you'll self-assess with IMSAFE and your personal minimums.

head: Symptoms
Condition
Fix
rows: Euphoria, headache, blue lips at altitude
Joint pain after a dive and a flight
100 percent oxygen, descend, land, see an AME [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Fatigue, headache, cramps in the heat

check.q: Name the cause and fix for nausea, sweating and paleness on an early lesson.
check.a: Motion sickness from mixed signals; open vents, look outside, limit head movement, tell your CFI [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

f1.caption: Figure 17-2. The Eustachian tube allows air pressure to equalize in the middle ear.
f1.alt: Cutaway of the ear showing outer ear, auditory canal, eardrum, middle ear, and the Eustachian tube running down to the opening in the throat.

f2.caption: Figure 17-4. Human sensation of angular acceleration.
f2.alt: Four inner-ear canal drawings: no turning gives no sensation, start of turn gives a turning sensation, a constant-rate turn gives no sensation, and stopping the turn gives a sensation of turning the opposite way.

f3.caption: Figure 17-5. Graveyard spiral.
f3.alt: An airplane in a descending tightening spiral (graveyard spiral) beside a spinning airplane (graveyard spin) ending in ground impact.

f4.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions.
f4.alt: Panels comparing normal and illusion-induced approach paths for narrower and wider runways and for downsloping and upsloping runways.

f5.caption: Figure 17-22. At night, the horizon may be hard to discern due to dark terrain and misleading light patterns on the ground.
f5.alt: Night view from a cockpit where a level line of ground lights looks like the horizon while the actual horizon is tilted.

f6.caption: Figure 17-8. Impairment scale with alcohol use.
f6.alt: Table of alcohol content in common drinks and blood alcohol ranges with their effects, from appearing normal up to unconsciousness and death.

f7.caption: Figure 2-20. The pilot has a certain capacity of doing work and handling tasks. However, there is a point where the tasking exceeds the pilot's capability.
f7.alt: Chart of task load over time from preflight to landing; the margin of safety between pilot capabilities and task requirements shrinks and disappears during approach and landing.

scenario.title: Saturday morning at the lake
scenario.setup: You plan a 90-minute solo cross-country Saturday at 8 a.m., cruising at 9,500 feet. Friday you made two no-stop scuba dives that ended at 3 p.m., then had two beers that ended at 11 p.m. You slept 5 hours, woke with a stuffy nose, and took a diphenhydramine (Benadryl) pill. Your family is driving to meet you at the destination for lunch. A friend says, "You'll be fine, you always are."

questions.q: Are you legal under 91.17 for alcohol?
questions.a: Yes on the 8-hour rule (9 hours since the last beer) if you're under 0.04 and not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. But AIM advises 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

questions.q: Can you fly at 9,500 feet after the dives?
questions.a: No. Above 8,000 feet you should wait at least 24 hours after any dive; you'll have only about 17 hours [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]].

questions.q: What about the stuffy nose and the pill?
questions.a: Flying with congestion risks ear and sinus block in descent [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in your system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]; 91.17 bans any drug that affects faculties contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

questions.q: Which hazardous attitude is your friend encouraging, and what is the external pressure?
questions.a: Invulnerability ("It won't happen to me"); antidote: "It could happen to me" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Family waiting is an external pressure, the factor most likely to make you ignore the rest [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

questions.q: Say you go anyway, with a lower plan. On arrival, the ATIS says a different runway than you always use. What's the trap?
questions.a: Expectation bias: hearing the usual runway instead of the one given. Fatigue makes it worse [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Read back and verify.

Don't fly today. IMSAFE fails on Illness, Medication, Alcohol (within 24 hours) and Fatigue [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. Call the family, reschedule, and drive or wait. Plan ahead to be ready for delays [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

skills.do: Given symptoms or a condition, link at least three of the K1a-K1l conditions to their cause(s) and corrective action(s), e.g. hypoxia, hyperventilation, CO poisoning, ear block, the leans, scuba DCS.
skills.practice: Make flash cards: symptoms on one side, condition + cause + fix on the other. Have a friend read symptoms aloud and answer in one sentence each.

skills.do: Do an honest self-assessment for the actual checkride flight or the examiner's scenario: run IMSAFE out loud, compare the conditions to your written personal minimums, and give a clear go or no-go with reasons.
skills.practice: Before every lesson, run IMSAFE and PAVE out loud with your CFI. Fill out the RMH personal minimums worksheet [[30:13|RMH 2-1]] and bring it to the checkride.

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.17, a pilot may not act as a crewmember within how many hours after drinking alcohol?
quiz.why: No crewmember duties within 8 hours of any alcoholic beverage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: What is the 91.17 alcohol concentration limit?
quiz.why: You may not fly with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater, so it must be less than 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]].

quiz.q: After a dive that required a controlled ascent, how long should you wait before flying at 6,500 feet MSL?
quiz.why: Decompression-stop diving needs at least 24 hours even for flight up to 8,000 feet [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]].

quiz.q: A pilot feels euphoric with a headache and blue fingernails at 14,000 feet. What is the best action?
options: Turn off the cabin heater only
Increase power and climb above the clouds
quiz.why: These are hypoxia symptoms; treat by flying lower and/or using oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

quiz.q: Which illusion makes a pilot feel the wings are level while in a descending, steady turn, leading them to pull back and tighten the spiral?
quiz.why: In a graveyard spiral the pilot senses a wings-level descent and pulls back, tightening the spiral [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

quiz.q: An upsloping runway tends to make a pilot fly what kind of approach?
quiz.why: Upslope makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

quiz.q: Which is the antidote for the macho attitude?
options: Follow the rules. They are usually right.
quiz.why: Macho ("I can do it") is countered by "Taking chances is foolish." [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]

quiz.q: How long should you wait after the first dose of a new over-the-counter medication before flying?
quiz.why: Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to make sure you have no adverse side effects [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

quiz.q: A pilot reads a NOTAM about a closed runway but still sees it as the old closure and lines up on the closed runway. This is an example of:
quiz.why: Perceiving information as it was before despite new evidence is expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

quiz.q: Within how many days must you report an alcohol-related motor vehicle action to the FAA?
quiz.why: A written report is due no later than 60 days after the motor vehicle action [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

takeaways: Preflight yourself with IMSAFE before every flight; pilot impairment causes more accidents than aircraft failures.
Alcohol: 8 hours AND under 0.04 is the legal floor; 12 to 24 hours is smart.
Scuba: 12 hours (no stops, up to 8,000 ft), 24 hours with stops or above 8,000 ft.
In clouds or at night, trust the instruments, not your body.
Know the five hazardous attitudes and say the antidote out loud.
When overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize; and double-check what you expect to hear.
cfi_notes: Examiners often give a scenario mixing legal and smart: e.g. 9 hours after drinking (legal) vs AIM's 12-24 hours (smart). Make students state both.
Students mix up hypoxia and hyperventilation. Teach the AIM order: if on oxygen, go to 100 percent and check the system first, then slow breathing (AIM 8-1-3c).

Source conflict: PHAK Figure 17-1 lists 30 minutes or more TUC at 20,000 ft, but AIM 8-1-2a says corrective ability is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft. Use the more conservative number and discuss. (PHAK says hypoxia symptoms differ from person to person; AIM 8-1-2a says they do not vary in an individual. These agree: each pilot tends to get the same symptoms every time, which is why altitude chamber training helps.)
Have students fill out the RMH personal minimums worksheet (RMH Ch 2) before solo cross-country, then bring it to the checkride for S2.
Demonstrate disorientation in flight only with an instructor at a safe altitude (PHAK 17-9); it makes the 'trust your instruments' point stick.
Common miss: students forget scuba waits apply to passengers too, and that the altitudes are actual MSL, not cabin altitude.
Students often think OTC means safe. Use the diphenhydramine example and the 48-hour / five-dosing-interval rules.
gaps: K1j Hypothermia: none of the provided resources (PHAK, AIM, RMH, AFH, 14 CFR, AC 60-22 full text) describe hypothermia symptoms, causes or treatment. Only related items were found (cold reduces circulation, PHAK 17-4; cold raises oxygen demand, AIM 8-1-2a; carry clothing and survival gear over remote areas, PHAK 2-9; appropriate clothing on AC 60-22's fitness checklist). The CFI must supply hypothermia content from another source.

K1i Nutrition: sources give only brief guidance (balanced meals, snacks, low blood sugar as a stressor, PHAK; protein meal/snack, noncarbonated fluids and the 'Eating' item of I'M SAFE, AC 60-22 par. 21f and Figure 7); no detailed nutrition guidance.

AC 60-22 (1991) is now fully readable (OCR, all 34 pages). Its hazardous attitudes and antidotes (par. 13-14, Figure 4) match PHAK Figure 2-4 and are cited; its stress-management, fitness checklist, and alcohol-duration content is used in the stress, nutrition and alcohol chunks. Its alcohol/marijuana durations and I'M SAFE 'Eating' version are older than current PHAK/AIM guidance, which this lesson treats as primary.

activities.title: Hypoxia, hyperventilation, or both?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Fixed by flying lower or using oxygen
Fixed by slowing your breathing or talking out loud

activities.title: Name that illusion
activities.intro: Tap an illusion, then what it makes you feel.

pairs.r: Banked the other way after leveling from a slow turn
Turning on a new axis after a head move in a long turn
Wings level while you descend in a steady turn
Nose-up during the fast speed-up of takeoff
Tumbling backward after leveling off from a climb
Climbing when an updraft lifts you

activities.title: True or false: alcohol and medicine

cards.s: Once 9 hours have passed since your last drink, you may fly no matter what a breath test shows.
cards.why: No. You also need an alcohol concentration below 0.04. At 0.04 or more after 8 hours, you wait until it drops [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

cards.s: A pilot with a hangover is still under the influence of alcohol.
cards.why: Yes. Motor and mental impairment are still there, even if you feel normal [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

cards.s: Altitude makes the effects of alcohol weaker.
cards.why: No. Altitude multiplies them: two drinks can act like three or four [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

cards.s: Aspirin, acetaminophen or ibuprofen at the correct dose usually does not stop you from flying.
cards.why: Yes. These OTC pain relievers have few side effects at correct doses, so flying usually is not restricted [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

cards.s: A sleepy-making medicine taken every 4 hours calls for a wait of at least 20 hours after the last dose.
cards.why: Yes. Wait at least five dosing intervals: 5 x 4 hours = 20 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

cards.s: In a state where marijuana is legal, pilots may use it as long as they wait 8 hours.
cards.why: No. The FAA says marijuana is an illicit drug under federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

activities.title: When to run the 5P check
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the 5P check points in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Preflight, before you load the airplane
Midpoint of the flight (hourly if over 2 hours)
Just before descent into the terminal area
Just before entering the traffic pattern (VFR)

final_quiz.q: You donated blood a few days before a flight. Which type of hypoxia are you more at risk for?
final_quiz.why: Hypemic hypoxia means the blood can't carry enough oxygen. Blood donation can cause it, and blood volume can take weeks to return to normal [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].

final_quiz.q: You are on supplemental oxygen at 14,000 feet when you start to feel lightheaded with tingling fingers. What should you do first?
options: Set the regulator to 100 percent oxygen and check the system works
Climb to get above any turbulence
final_quiz.why: Early hypoxia and hyperventilation feel alike and can happen together. On oxygen, go to 100 percent and check the system first, then slow your breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3c]].

final_quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent an ear or sinus block?
options: Don't fly with a cold or a nasal allergy
Use a decongestant spray before every flight
Take an oral decongestant before takeoff
Descend as fast as you can to get it over with
final_quiz.why: The block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy. Sprays and drops usually don't protect enough, and oral decongestants can impair you [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2b]].

final_quiz.q: Flying in haze with no clear horizon, you slowly drift into a left bank without noticing. When you level the wings, you feel banked to the right. What is this, and what do you do?
options: Coriolis illusion; move your head quickly to reset it
Autokinesis; stare at one fixed light
The leans; trust the attitude indicator and keep the wings level
final_quiz.why: A slow bank below the inner ear's detection limit, then leveling, causes the leans: a false feeling of banking the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Trust the instruments, not your body [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

final_quiz.q: You usually land on a 75-foot-wide runway. Today you fly to an airport with a 150-foot-wide runway. What error should you watch for?
options: Leveling off too high and landing hard
Flying a low approach and landing short
final_quiz.why: A wider-than-usual runway makes you feel lower than you are, so you fly high, risking leveling out high and landing hard or overshooting [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

final_quiz.q: On a cold day with the heater on, your passenger gets a headache and feels dizzy. You smell no exhaust. What should you do?
options: Nothing yet, since CO always has a strong smell
Turn the heater up so the passenger stays warm
Turn off the heater, open the fresh air vents and windows, and use oxygen if you have it
Climb higher to get cooler air
final_quiz.why: CO is colorless and odorless, so no smell does not mean no CO. Turn off the heater, open vents and windows, and use oxygen if available [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Get medical help if symptoms are severe or last after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4c]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a 2-hour flight in severe summer heat. Using the PHAK guide, about how much water should you drink during the flight?
options: Only what you need when you feel thirsty
final_quiz.why: Drink one quart per hour in severe heat: 2 hours x 1 quart = 2 quarts. Don't wait for thirst [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your passenger made a scuba dive with no decompression stops that ended at 10 a.m. You plan to cruise at 5,500 feet MSL. What is the earliest recommended departure time?
final_quiz.why: For flight up to 8,000 feet after a no-stop dive, wait at least 12 hours: 10 a.m. plus 12 hours is 10 p.m. The rule applies to passengers too [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2d]].

final_quiz.q: Before a flight, a passenger shows up clearly drunk. It is not an emergency, and they are not a medical patient. What does 14 CFR 91.17 say?
options: You may carry them if they sit in the back
You may carry them if they are not a crewmember
You may carry them if the flight is under 1 hour
You may not let them be carried in the aircraft
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated to be carried (medical patients under proper care excepted) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your doctor prescribes a medicine to take every 8 hours. It can make you dizzy. After your last dose, how long should you wait before flying?
final_quiz.why: For a medicine with possible side effects like sedation or dizziness, wait at least five dosing intervals: 5 x 8 hours = 40 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot reads about a new temporary flight restriction and says, "Rules like that are silly. No one can tell me where to fly." Which attitude and antidote fit?
options: Anti-authority: "Follow the rules. They are usually right."
final_quiz.why: Seeing rules as silly and not wanting anyone to say what to do is anti-authority. Its antidote is "Follow the rules. They are usually right." [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]

final_quiz.q: Entering busy airspace, you notice you are working harder but getting less done, and you keep staring at one radio. What should you do?
options: Speed up so you get through it faster
Stop, think, slow down, and prioritize
Turn off the radios to cut the noise
Focus on the one task until it is done
final_quiz.why: Working harder but getting less done is the first sign of overload. The fix is to stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. You can also ask ATC for a delay or vectors to buy time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot is sure the weather ahead will improve. A new pilot report says the ceilings are dropping, but the pilot ignores it because it doesn't fit the plan. What is this?
final_quiz.why: Pushing away information that doesn't fit what you already believe is confirmation bias, instead of triggering an internal "uh-oh" [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your baseline personal minimum ceiling is 3,000 feet. Today you are tired after a long workday. Using the RMH adjustment table, what should your ceiling minimum be at least?
final_quiz.why: For illness, medication, stress or fatigue, the RMH says add at least 500 feet to the ceiling: 3,000 + 500 = 3,500 feet [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]].
